subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Ancient Greek Astronomy
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Ancient Greek Astronomy.

hook.text: Ancient Greeks didn't just watch the sky—they tried to explain it. They asked why the cosmos works as it does.

buildup.text: Aristotle argued Earth was the center of the universe. Ptolemy built a detailed model that lasted 1,400 years.

discovery.text: Aristarchus proposed the Sun was at the center around 250 BC. He was right—but nobody believed him for 1,800 years.

twist.text: Eratosthenes measured Earth's circumference using shadows and geometry. He was accurate to within 2% of the true value.

climax.text: Greek astronomy combined observation with reasoning. This shift from recording to explaining changed science forever.

punchline.text: From watching to wondering why. The Greeks invented scientific astronomy.

quiz.question: Who first proposed that the Sun, not Earth, was at the center?

details.summary: Greek astronomers (600 BCE-200 CE) revolutionized astronomy by seeking physical explanations for celestial phenomena rather than only divine ones. Aristarchus proposed a Sun-centered model, Eratosthenes measured Earth's circumference, and Hipparchus cataloged 850 stars.
details.whyItMatters: Greek astronomy introduced the idea that the universe operates by natural laws that can be discovered through reason and observation — the philosophical foundation of all modern science.
takeaways: Greeks sought physical explanations for celestial phenomena
Aristarchus first proposed a Sun-centered model of the cosmos
Ptolemy's geocentric model dominated astronomy for 1,400 years

faq.question: How did Eratosthenes measure Earth's circumference?
faq.answer: Around 240 BCE, he noticed the Sun was directly overhead in Syene (Aswan) on the summer solstice but cast shadows in Alexandria. By measuring the shadow angle (about 7.2°) and knowing the distance between the cities, he calculated Earth's circumference — remarkably close to the actual value.

faq.question: Why was Aristarchus's heliocentric model rejected?
faq.answer: It couldn't explain why stars didn't show parallax (apparent shifting) if Earth moved — actually because stars are incredibly far away. Aristotle's physics also required a stationary Earth.
